question: In orbital cellulitis, a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) is a sign of optic nerve compromise and mandates urgent surgical decompression regardless of the Chandler classification stage.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This is true. The presence of a RAPD in orbital cellulitis is a sight-threatening emergency. It indicates posterior optic nerve ischaemia or compression, which can lead to permanent visual loss within hours. RAPD overrides staging — urgent surgery is indicated.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. A RAPD indicates optic nerve dysfunction and is an ophthalmic emergency regardless of Chandler stage. Even if the infection is 'only' Class II or III by imaging, an RAPD signals imminent visual loss from nerve ischaemia or compression. Emergency IV steroids and surgical decompression (drainage of abscess ± orbital decompression) must not be delayed while awaiting 24–48 h of antibiotic response.
